file_summaries.title: Common Errors in CuTe DSL
critical_patterns: Type Errors: Missing annotations, wrong types
Memory Errors: Out of bounds, alignment issues
Synchronization Errors: Missing barriers, race conditions
Compilation Errors: Syntax, imports, JIT issues
code_snippets:
@cute.kernel
def with_sync():
    smem = cute.make_smem_tensor(cute.make_shape(256), cutlass.Float32)
    tid = cute.arch.thread_idx()[0]
    smem[tid] = tid
    cute.arch.syncthreads()
    value = smem[(tid + 1) % 256]
constraints: All kernel parameters must have type annotations
Use CuTe types, not Python types in kernels
Maximum threads per block is 1024 on most GPUs
Block size should be multiple of warp size (32) for efficiency
Ensure all threads in block reach syncthreads()
file_summaries.compressed_summary: This guide addresses common errors encountered while writing CuTe DSL kernels, focusing on type, memory, launch, synchronization, and compilation errors. Type errors often arise from missing annotations or using Python types instead of CuTe types. Memory errors include out-of-bounds access and uninitialized memory, which can be mitigated by bounds checking and proper initialization. Launch configuration errors typically involve exceeding the maximum threads per block or using non-warp-multiple block sizes. Synchronization errors, such as missing syncthreads or conditional sync leading to deadlocks, require careful use of barriers. Compilation errors often stem from incorrect imports or unsupported Python constructs in JIT compilation. Key practices include ensuring type annotations, validating grid/block dimensions, and synchronizing before accessing shared memory. Use validation functions and follow a checklist to prevent errors. Always test with small inputs and carefully analyze error messages for efficient debugging.

file_summaries.title: Debugging Techniques for CuTe DSL
critical_patterns: Start with the simplest possible test to isolate issues quickly.
Use print statements selectively to avoid output spam.
Employ runtime assertions to check invariants within kernels.
Validate inputs and outputs before and after kernel execution.
Compare kernel outputs with a reference implementation to identify discrepancies.
Incrementally build and test kernel components to isolate bugs.
code_snippets:
def validate_and_launch(kernel, data, expected_min=None, expected_max=None):
    print("Pre-launch validation:")
    print(f"  Shape: {data.shape}")
    kernel.launch(grid=[10,1,1], block=[256,1,1])(cute.from_dlpack(data))

@cute.kernel
def complex_kernel(data: cute.Tensor):
    tid = cute.arch.thread_idx()[0]
    value = data[tid]
    cute.printf("After load: %f\n", value)
    value = process_a(value)
    cute.printf("After process_a: %f\n", value)
constraints: Avoid debugging with large datasets; use small test cases.
Ensure print statements are controlled to prevent excessive output.
Always validate kernel inputs and outputs for NaN or Inf values.
Use systematic debugging approaches to isolate bugs efficiently.
Incremental development helps in identifying which change introduces a bug.
file_summaries.compressed_summary: Debugging GPU kernels using CuTe DSL involves several strategic approaches to efficiently identify and resolve issues. Key techniques include print debugging, runtime assertions, isolating problems, reducing test cases, and comparing outputs with reference implementations. Start with the simplest possible test case to quickly isolate issues, and use print statements selectively to avoid output spam. Assertions can be used within kernels to check for invariant conditions, helping to catch errors early. Validate inputs and outputs before and after kernel execution to ensure data integrity. Comparing kernel outputs with a known-good reference implementation is crucial for identifying discrepancies. Incremental development is recommended, where each component is built and tested separately to isolate bugs effectively. Tools like cuda-memcheck, compute-sanitizer, and cuda-gdb are valuable for detecting memory errors, race conditions, and performance bottlenecks. The systematic approach involves observing the problem, hypothesizing potential causes, testing with added checks, analyzing results, making targeted fixes, and verifying the solution. This structured method, combined with practical debugging tools, forms the backbone of effective debugging in CuTe DSL.

essential_patterns: Use type annotations to prevent type errors, ensuring that CuTe types are used instead of Python types.
Validate grid and block dimensions to avoid launch configuration errors, ensuring they do not exceed hardware limits.
Implement bounds checking and proper initialization to mitigate memory errors such as out-of-bounds access.
Use synchronization primitives like syncthreads correctly to prevent deadlocks and ensure proper execution order.
Apply incremental development and isolate components to efficiently identify and resolve issues.
Utilize debugging tools like cuda-memcheck and cuda-gdb to detect memory errors and race conditions.
common_pitfalls: Missing type annotations leading to type errors
Out-of-bounds memory access due to improper bounds checking
Exceeding maximum threads per block in launch configurations
Using unsupported Python constructs in JIT compilation
compressed_overview: Debugging in CuTe DSL involves understanding and addressing various types of errors that can occur during kernel development. Common errors include type errors from missing annotations, memory errors such as out-of-bounds access, launch configuration errors from exceeding hardware limits, and synchronization errors leading to deadlocks. Effective debugging techniques include print debugging, using assertions to catch invariant violations, and comparing outputs with reference implementations. Incremental development and isolating components help in pinpointing issues. Essential practices involve validating inputs and outputs, ensuring proper use of synchronization primitives, and leveraging debugging tools like cuda-memcheck and cuda-gdb for detecting memory errors and race conditions. By following a systematic approach to debugging and adhering to best practices, developers can efficiently identify and resolve issues in CuTe DSL kernels.
